claims.text: Structural and chemical stability across 473–1923 K is governed by competition between entropy-stabilizing sluggish diffusion and temperature-activated atomic reordering or oxidation.
At lower temperatures, high configurational entropy maintains a single-phase solid solution.
Increasing temperature increases atomic mobility sufficiently to initiate short-range chemical ordering.
Increasing temperature can initiate selective surface oxidation.
Short-range ordering or selective surface oxidation can destabilize nanoparticle structure.
The initial material is an equal- or near-equal-ratio alloy of at least five metals crystallized as a single-phase solid solution.
Temperature-activated atomic diffusion produces short-range-order clusters.
Temperature-activated processes produce a surface oxide layer.
Configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion kinetically inhibit atomic segregation at lower temperatures.
At higher temperatures, atomic mobility overcomes the kinetic barrier to local chemical reordering.
Local chemical reordering changes thermoelectric-relevant transport behavior.
Nanoparticles retain a single-phase high-entropy solid solution up to a critical temperature.
Catalytic and thermoelectric performance remains consistent up to that critical temperature.
Above the critical temperature, short-range ordering or surface oxidation becomes observable.
The onset of short-range ordering or surface oxidation correlates with deterioration of structural integrity.
The onset of short-range ordering or surface oxidation correlates with deterioration of catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
Initial room-temperature nanoparticles have homogeneous single-phase structures.
Initial room-temperature nanoparticles have uniform catalytic and thermoelectric properties.
Instability is expected mainly near the upper end of the operating range, close to 1923 K.
Sufficient environmental oxygen promotes oxidation and therefore lowers stability.
